tts: For thousands of years, ever since the Greek philosopher Plato identified them, people have divided the taste of food into four types: sweet, sour, bitter and salty.

However, in 1908 a Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, sensed that his seaweed soup had a flavour which was not one of the classic four. He knew that the flavour was also found in tomatoes, in hard cheese such as Parmesan, and in meat — though not so much in very lean or raw meat.
Eventually he identified it as glutamic acid, but he named it umami, which means delicious in Japanese.

Umami is best described as a kind of savoury taste which makes something taste really good. It is very noticeable in many Asian foods, such as soya, asparagus, shrimp and green tea, but it is also strong in foods which combine meat, cheese and tomato — Italian meatballs, or a cheeseburger with tomato ketchup.

items.q: What is umami?
o: A fifth basic taste, best described as savoury

items.q: Who identified it, and when?
Where is it strong?
o: In foods combining meat, cheese and tomato

tts: Umami encourages people to eat, which may be why it is now added to many foods in the form of monosodium glutamate.

It may also affect your choice of drinks on an aeroplane. According to Charles Spence, professor of experimental psychology at Oxford, tomato juice should taste better than other drinks in the air, and in fact many people on aeroplanes do seem to choose it.
This could be because the noise of the aircraft reduces our ability to taste sweetness and increases our sensitivity to umami.
Sound affects taste in other ways too. Crisps come in noisy packets because the sound adds to the sensation of crunchiness, and some music can make food taste less salty.

items.s: Umami encourages people to eat more.
Monosodium glutamate is added to food to increase savoury taste.
Aircraft noise is thought to increase our sensitivity to sweetness.
Noisy packets are thought to increase the sensation of crunchiness.
Music has no measurable effect on taste.

tts: There was research a few years back into the world’s funniest joke by a group who called themselves LaughLab. They received over forty thousand jokes from a number of different countries.
People from Ireland, the UK, Australia and New Zealand showed a strong preference for jokes with wordplay or a pun — where a word has two meanings.
Americans and Canadians seemed to prefer jokes where somebody looked stupid, or was made to look stupid by another person.
Many European countries, such as France, Denmark and Belgium, liked to make a joke out of topics that usually make us feel anxious, like illness and death.
What one person thinks is hilarious, another might find really distasteful, or just annoying.

acts.title: Doing it, and having it happen to you
rule: English splits the senses in two. One set of verbs describes something you do on purpose — look, watch, listen. The other describes something that simply reaches you — see, hear. Most languages do not make the split this sharply, which is why this is a lifelong error for many learners.
points: see vs look at vs watch
see = it reaches your eyes. look at = you direct your eyes. watch = you follow something that moves or changes over time.
hear = the sound reaches you. listen to = you direct your attention. listen always takes to before an object.
glance at (quickly), gaze at (long, admiring), stare at (long, often rude), glare at (angrily).
These work both ways. It tastes salty is what reaches you; I tasted the soup is what you did.
taste of + the actual substance; taste like + a comparison. It tastes of lemon; it tastes like soap.
No continuous for the receiving sense
I see the problem, not I am seeing the problem — unless see means meet.
eg: I saw her on the bus this morning.
It reached my eyes; I did not plan it.
I looked at the photograph for a long time.
Deliberate, and it changes over time.
I was listening to the radio.
Don’t stare at people in public.
She glared at me every time I spoke.
It tastes like something my grandmother made.
acts.careful: “I am seeing a bird outside” is wrong unless you have an appointment with it. see for the receiving sense has no continuous form; use I can see.

write.q: Describe a place through the senses in about 180 words — a market, a café, a kitchen, a station. Keep the deliberate verbs and the receiving verbs apart: say what you looked at and what you simply saw, what you listened to and what you heard. Use at least three of the precise looking verbs, and both taste of and taste like.
plan: what you saw without looking for it
what you heard, and what you listened to
write.model:
The first thing I saw when I came in was the queue, which went past the bread and turned the corner. I had not been looking for it; it was simply the whole room.

What I looked at properly, once I had joined it, was the woman at the front counting coins onto the counter. Everybody behind her glanced at her and then very deliberately looked away, which is a national skill.

I could hear at least four conversations and was listening to none of them until somebody behind me said my surname, at which point I stared at the ceiling and listened extremely carefully. It was not me.

The bread there tastes of the wood in the oven, which sounds like something written on a menu and is simply true. My grandmother’s tasted like it and never quite the same, and I have never worked out what the difference was.
